Working outline. Sections marked **[RESULT]** depend on data not yet collected.

---

## 1. Introduction

The reliability of V-Dem's democracy scores depends on panel size. When a country-year has
13 coders, the IRT posterior is well-identified and robust to outliers. When it has 2, a
single high-reliability coder anchors the estimate and the posterior is barely
distinguishable from the hierarchical prior.

Three distinct pathologies motivate the problem:

- **Historical sparsity**: 59% of pre-1990 country-years have ≤3 distinct coders.
  V-Dem's retrospective coding relied on 1–2 country specialists who coded entire
  national histories back to 1789. Major democracies (Germany, France, UK) have 100+
  years of 2-coder panels. Pre-1900 cross-national comparisons largely reflect the
  model's prior beliefs, not the data.

- **Chronic thin coverage**: ~35 contemporary countries have mean panel size < 8 in
  2010–2024 — predominantly small island states, small African states, and
  hard-access authoritarian regimes.

- **Leading-edge attrition**: post-2013 coder cohorts are aging out without
  replacement. Annual attrition of 45–133 coders with near-zero new recruitment.
  Median panel size ~5.8 by 2024, returning to pre-2005 levels. The most urgent
  and universal gap. See `analysis/01-panel-degradation-pathologies.qmd` for
  the full empirical picture.

The paper asks: can AI-generated ratings substitute for human expert coders in V-Dem's
measurement system? Specifically: which prompt strategy and model scale produces the most
calibrated AI ratings, and does a fine-tuned model generalize to indicators it was not
trained on?

---

## 2. Background

### V-Dem's measurement model

V-Dem pools ordinal ratings from multiple expert coders through an IRT model that
estimates latent country-year democracy scores while simultaneously modeling coder
reliability (β) and threshold placement (γ). Adding a coder moves the posterior from
prior-dominated to data-informed — but only if the added ratings are sufficiently
similar to existing human ratings that they do not shift the panel mean detectably.

### Prior work on AI annotation

- Gilardi et al. (2023): GPT-3.5 matches or exceeds crowd-workers on political text
  annotation — but crowd-workers are not calibrated domain experts.
- LLM-as-survey-respondent literature (Bisbee et al.; Argyle et al.): AI can
  approximate aggregate human opinion distributions. Not directly applicable —
  we are not trying to simulate opinion, but to apply globally calibrated expert
  standards to observable political conditions.
- Bridge-coder companion paper: AI as cross-national calibration tool (bridge coder).
  Different problem from this paper — that paper tests whether AI can link
  disconnected national panels via IRT thresholds; this paper tests substitution
  within panels.

---

## 3. Research design

### Prompt conditions (3)

1. **Codebook-only**: global framing + V-Dem codebook question and response categories.
   No source text. Measures the calibration signal available from pretraining alone.

2. **Evidence**: adds section-extracted State Department and Freedom House text, plus
   five few-shot calibration examples (one per ordinal level, globally distributed).

3. **Anonymized**: same as Evidence but an LLM agent replaces all country-identifying
   labels (names, cities, parties, leaders, organizations) with generic equivalents
   before the coding call. Few-shot examples are also anonymized. Tests whether
   country-identity shortcuts drive the compression bias observed in preliminary results.

### Models (5)

| Model | Scale | Platform |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | Frontier | Claude API |
| Llama 405B Instruct | 405B open | GW Pegasus |
| Llama 3.3 70B Instruct | 70B open | GW Pegasus |
| Llama 3.2 9B Instruct | 9B open | GW Pegasus |
| Llama 3.3 70B (fine-tuned) | 70B ft | GW Pegasus |

Fine-tuned Llama 70B is trained on (anonymized section text, individual coder rating)
pairs from V-Dem v15, 2013–2018, covering all strong + partial coverage Type C indicators
(~174 indicators). Uses the same anonymized prompt format without the few-shot block.

### Evaluation

Primary: **LOO MAE** — AI error against the panel mean vs. the typical error of a
held-out human coder against the rest of their panel. Bootstrap CIs (B=500) at the
CYI level. If AI LOO MAE ≈ human LOO MAE, the AI performs within the range of normal
human disagreement.

Secondary: exact match rate; adjacent-category agreement (within ±1 of rounded panel
mean).

Diagnostic: **signed deviation by democracy quintile** — detects directional compression
bias (rating autocracies too high, democracies too low).

### Evaluation indicator set

25–30 indicators selected for inference (3–4 per module), spanning coverage tiers from
strong to weak. Coverage tier (strong / partial / weak) enters as a moderating variable
in the results: the gradient from strong to weak coverage indicators is the within-study
test of how well the model generalizes beyond the evidence its prompts can anchor.
Exact indicator list determined after qualitative review of section-to-indicator
assignments; locked before any inference runs.

### Country-year pool

Primary: 2019 — one year after the training window closes, full panels, no COVID
distortion. Robustness: 2024 (best model only, thin-panel deployment simulation).

---

## 4. Results (anticipated)

### 4.1 Calibration table

**[RESULT]** LOO MAE by model × indicator, with human LOO baseline. Primary display:
forest plot with paired AI and human LOO MAE estimates per indicator (or difference
from human baseline centered on zero). Supplementary table: rows = 5 models + human
baseline, columns = 25–30 indicators grouped by module, with coverage tier noted.

Expected pattern: Evidence > Codebook-only; fine-tuned ≈ or > Anonymized; strong-
coverage indicators easier than weak-coverage. Whether anonymization helps or hurts
vs. Evidence is not predetermined — the direction of the country-identity effect is
an empirical question. Coverage tier gradient within the indicator set is the
within-study generalization test.

### 4.2 Compression diagnostic

**[RESULT]** Signed deviation by quintile, one line per model × condition. Expected:
without anonymization, AI rates Q1 autocracies too generously and Q5 democracies too
harshly (compression toward the middle). Anonymization should reduce this if
country-identity is the mechanism.

### 4.3 Coverage-tier moderation

**[RESULT]** LOO MAE by coverage tier (strong / partial / weak) across the evaluation
indicator set, for the best-performing model. Does calibration quality degrade
systematically as source coverage weakens? If the gradient is shallow, the result
supports a general V-Dem AI coder — trained on strong + partial indicators, it
generalizes to weaker-evidence indicators without per-indicator fine-tuning.

### 4.4 Integration robustness (k=1 replacement check)

**[RESULT]** For all 2019 CYIs with ≥8 coders: `|mean(panel + AI) − mean(panel)|`.
Bootstrap B=500. If mean divergence CI includes zero, adding one AI coder does not
detectably shift the panel mean. Reported as supplemental.

### 4.5 Exploratory and sensitivity analyses

**Persona variation** **[RESULT if run]**: two persona conditions (strict / lenient
framing) applied to the best-performing fine-tuned model on a subset of high-observability
indicators. Pre-registered as exploratory. If persona conditions produce reliable,
directional shifts in ratings, they provide a route to genuinely distinct AI panel
members for k=2/k=3 replacement. If not, the result contributes to evidence that
persona prompting does not shift ordinal ratings in structured expert-coding tasks.
Report: signed deviation (strict − neutral) and (lenient − neutral) by indicator and
democracy quintile.

**Temperature sensitivity**: best model re-run at temperature 0.7 on the calibration
pool. The spread of ratings across draws is a measure of model uncertainty. Reported as
a diagnostic in supplementary materials; not used as a source of distinct panel members
in the main replacement experiment.

---

## 5. Contributions

### Political science / democracy measurement

- Practical answer to an operational V-Dem problem: which AI strategy and model scale
  is safe to use for panel augmentation?
- Evidence-based guidance for three deployment scenarios: historical sparse panels
  (1975–1989), chronically thin contemporary panels (~35 countries), and the leading-
  edge attrition gap (post-2020).
- Generalization result — whether LOO MAE degrades across the strong → weak coverage
  gradient — motivates (or cautions against) application to the full ~216 Type C
  V-Dem indicator set without indicator-specific fine-tuning.

### NLP / AI annotation

- LOO benchmarking framework: frames AI annotation quality in terms of human
  inter-rater disagreement rather than deviation from a fixed gold label. Applicable
  to any multi-annotator annotation setting.
- Empirical test of fine-tuning generalization for structured ordinal expert annotation
  — a relatively understudied task type compared to classification and generation.
- Anonymization as a controlled test of identity-based shortcuts in LLM coding: does
  stripping country labels improve or degrade calibration?

### Practical guidance

The results will likely support a tiered recommendation:

- **Codebook + frontier model**: sufficient for quick, low-volume coding or initial
  exploration when fine-tuning is not feasible. If frontier models already produce
  well-calibrated ratings from codebook text alone, the evidence pipeline is
  unnecessary for many use cases.

- **Evidence + few-shot + large open model**: a practical middle ground for users who
  have source documents and GPU access but cannot invest in fine-tuning.

- **Fine-tuned model at scale**: highest calibration for systematic, large-volume
  deployment. Worth the investment when coding thousands of country-years across the
  full indicator set.

The crossover point — where the added cost of fine-tuning is justified by the
calibration gain — is itself a finding the paper can report.

---

## 6. Relation to companion paper

The bridge-coder paper (Political Analysis target) addresses cross-national calibration
via IRT: can AI link disconnected national panels by acting as a bridge coder across
country pairs? That paper's contribution is about threshold stability (γ); this paper's
contribution is about substitution (adding AI to a panel without shifting the mean).

Both papers share source documents, section extraction, and the anonymization pipeline.
Fine-tuning is secondary in the bridge-coder paper; it is a primary condition here.
